IBM Maximo Pricing Estimator

Redesigning the quote-to-deal workflow for IBM Maximo sellers to cut down 30% deal process time with enterprise clients within 3 months of launch.

Role

UX Designer

Timeline

Feb - Jul 2026

— THE PROBLEM

Broken workflow, held together by people

Maximo's AppPoints pricing confuses buyers before they reach a seller, then leaves sellers acting as the integration between five tools in their manual workflow.

Nothing in between absorbs the complexity for the people who have to use it.

Maximo Pricing page on ibm.com does not give the user an idea of what AppPoints are, leading to a lot of confusion when they talk to a seller and get introduced to the AppPoints concept.

The quoting tool was the AppPoints Calculator - a versioned Excel file emailed between teams, requiring manual copy-paste into CPQ, manual approval routing, and manual version control across Slack, email, IBM Sales Cloud, Salesforce, etc…

— SOLUTION

Three phases, one IBM goal

Phase 1:
AI layer built on watsonx Orchestrate

Feb – May 2026, private preview June 2026

First baby-step

For phase 1 - we focused on giving the seller a guided, conversation-style workflow, and the logic maps and generates a CPQ-ready quote automatically. The best thing is no manual copy-paste or any outdated spreadsheet versions.

Key outcomes so far:

95%

of quotes approved in ≤ 2 hours by the L0 approval team

Phase 2:
Unified pricing estimator

Jun - Jul 2026, private preview Jul. 2026

A unified workflow

I designed and built an internal tool which replaces the full fragmented stack—Excel, CPQ, Slack, email—with a single AI-powered workflow covering pricing, costing, and provisioning configuration.

A plain-language chat, built on IBM watsonx layer, that builds a Maximo quote from a deal description, and learning about Maximo concepts.

Phase 3:
Public pricing experience on ibm.com

A simpler concept

I built an exploratory concept to reimagine the public pricing experience, transforming it from a static list of technical add-ons into a guided, self-service estimator.

Launch Pricing prototype

How this helps:

> 5 mins

For the customer to estimate their costs and realizing the benefits of operational cost-saving (Usability testing, Sept. 26).

Main decisions

Clearer customer-facing language and form progressive disclosure

Before:

Unclear explanation and boundaries between tiers, leaving buyers guessing which capabilities belong in Essentials vs. Standard.

After:

Form with progressive disclosure, with clearer mapped business capabilities to package editions with plain-language explanations.

Explanations where customers need the most

Before:

Confronts users with technical line items like "non-production environments" and unguided user add-ons with verbose explanation.

After:

Grounds estimation in operational reality: Users simply specify the number of field technicians, operations managers, and administrators they have

Calculating customers' benefits

Before:

Laid out dozens of numbers and variables all at once with the assumption that users could digest them at a glance, resulting in data overload rather than clear ROI.

After:

Guides users through progressive disclosure, with digestible steps and focusing output numbers directly on the tangible business value Maximo delivers.

Extra: Benefits report for Executives

A sales and value-case piece for IBM Maximo, which can be downloaded and prepared in one printable page, it shows an executive why expanding Maximo is worth it.

Side note:

This redesigned pricing page is an exploratory vision prototype created to demonstrate how IBM could communicate value and pricing transparency to prospective clients. It has yet to fully resolve the underlying AppPoints licensing complexity, which remains a systemic product and business challenge.

— THE PROCESS

How the solution came together

This is a deep-dive into my research and process that shaped the Estimator vision itself, as well as tradeoffs.

Research

I ran in-depth interviews with 8 sellers (SMEs, ecosystem leaders, global sales) and 4 Customer Success Engineers (CSEs), who see the quote from the other side of the handoff. Clients don't care about AppPoints. They want to know what they're paying and what they get.

"Most of our customers are actually confused at just what an AppPoint is, much less the pricing calculator."

— IBM seller

Apart from the tooling problem, in fact, every seller built their own tools: custom calculators, questionnaires, scoping decks,… because the official one was too complex to share with clients.

"It is a hot mess. I do not show the pricing calculator to the clients at all... There's no integration between systems right now. The integration is me."

— IBM seller

Constraints that shaped the solution

The other idea I had was to connect everything: sync Excel, CPQ, Salesforce, and Gainsight into one integrated system.

However…

"If you're in a startup you can go live tomorrow. But this is IBM…it takes at least 6 months to 2 years…"

— Asset Lifecycle Management PM

Also, sellers already had too many tools both 1st and 3rd party, so it wouldn't be good to introduce another.

Re-purposing the chatbot

The insight that shaped the unified estimator was that sellers didn't want a chatbot. They wanted something that would let them control the quote.

And then, this becomes the prerequisite to the AI Assistant in the Estimator itself.

Validation

I ran unmoderated usability testing with the same previous participants. testing realistic enterprise quoting scenarios (new deals, trade-ups, and mixed authorized/concurrent user pools).

"I don't have to second-guess whether I broke it or using an outdated Excel file."

— Maximo field seller

"I can actually run through this on a call along with a client and get a clean quote in minutes instead of hours."

— Customer success manager

Lessons learned

"Just because you can build it, doesn't make it a good idea"

Now that I can build pretty much anything quickly with AI, it's important to know how to strip out the junk and focus on what's more important.

I've developed a mindset to plan things and organize artifacts more efficiently, not just to waste tokens, but also ship what's important and scalable to prevent technical debt long-term.

The corporate rule

IBM also taught me that design decisions have to survive months of alignment meetings and handoffs you can't predict. Delivery with speed is important, but longevity rules above all.

What I'd do differently

It's impossible to boil the ocean now that the whole architecture of Maximo was built around AppPoints. Inside the product (Maximo) itself, there could potentially be ways to let users learn about the AppPoints concept better.

One proposed concept - "AppPoints nudge" with explanation tooltip. I borrowed inspirations from AI token usage.

Project-wise, I would push for validation plans as soon as possible since we were testing out concepts really quickly but the time for alignment meetings were taking up a large portion of the roadmaps. Therefore, we could know where problems were and what could've been done to improve quicker.

The project prototypes were made possible with IBM Bob.
